questions.q: What is the key difference between cron/Windows Task Scheduler and an in-process scheduler like APScheduler?
options: cron only works on Windows, while APScheduler only works on Linux
cron and Task Scheduler trigger a program at the OS level independent of any running process, while APScheduler runs inside a long-lived Python process and can schedule jobs dynamically from code
APScheduler cannot run jobs more than once
cron requires a GUI, while APScheduler is command-line only
questions.explain: cron and Task Scheduler are OS-level mechanisms that run independent of any particular process; APScheduler runs inside a Python process, trading OS independence for the ability to add/remove jobs dynamically and share state with the running application.

questions.q: What does it mean for a scheduled job to be idempotent?
options: The job runs faster each time it is executed
The job can only be run once per calendar day
Running the job twice, or re-running it after a failure, produces the same correct end state rather than duplicated or corrupted output
The job never logs any output
questions.explain: Idempotency is about safety under re-runs: a job that overwrites a dated snapshot or upserts by key produces the same correct state no matter how many times it runs, while a job that blindly appends a new row every run is not idempotent.

questions.q: Why is a job that appends a new row to a table every time it runs, with no deduplication, NOT idempotent?
options: Because appending rows is always slower than overwriting a file
Because running it twice (e.g. after an accidental re-run) produces a duplicate row, meaning the end state depends on how many times it happened to run rather than converging to one correct state
Because tables cannot have more than one row with the same values
Because APScheduler blocks jobs that write to tables
questions.explain: An append-only job without deduplication accumulates a duplicate every time it's accidentally re-run, so the end state is not stable under re-runs -- the defining failure of non-idempotent design.

questions.q: In the APScheduler example, what does `max_instances=1` prevent?
options: The scheduler from ever stopping once started
The job from running more than once total
A slow-running execution of the job from overlapping with the next scheduled trigger, which could let two concurrent runs corrupt the same output
The log messages from including a timestamp
questions.explain: max_instances=1 ensures that if a run takes longer than the scheduled interval, the next trigger won't start a second overlapping execution -- important because concurrent overlapping runs against the same output can break idempotency.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize logging and alerting for unattended scheduled jobs specifically?
options: Because logging is required by APScheduler's API to function at all
Because no one is watching an unattended job fail in real time, so the job itself must make failures visible with enough context to diagnose, and alert somewhere a human will actually notice
Because scheduled jobs cannot raise exceptions
Because cron automatically emails a log file after every run
questions.explain: An unattended job's only way of surfacing a problem is through logs and alerts, since there's no person watching it execute -- clear, context-rich logging (tying back to Chapter 4's logging practices) and real alerting are what make a failure diagnosable rather than silently missed.
